nameStory: The Giant Leopard Moth gets its name from its stunning spotted pattern that looks remarkably like a leopard's coat! Its bright white wings are decorated with bold black spots and blotches, creating one of nature's most striking animal prints. The 'giant' part comes from its impressive 3-inch wingspan, making it one of our larger moths.
description: The Giant Leopard Moth is a spectacular large moth with brilliant white wings covered in neat black spots and blotches. Adults have a wingspan of about 3 inches, with males being noticeably larger than females. Their bodies are equally eye-catching, featuring dark blue abdomens with bright orange markings and distinctive black-and-white banded legs. These nocturnal beauties are strictly night fliers and belong to the tiger moth family.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Bright white wings with crisp black spots and blotches - some spots are solid while others are hollow rings, creating a leopard-like pattern that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Body Coloration
idTips.description: Dark blue abdomen with vivid orange markings on top and white underside with black spots - the colors are surprisingly vibrant and metallic-looking

idTips.label: Leg Pattern
idTips.description: Black and white banded legs that look like striped stockings - the bands are clearly defined and very noticeable when the moth is at rest

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large moth with 3-inch wingspan - males are bigger at 2 inches long while females are smaller at just over 1 inch long

idTips.label: Flight Time
idTips.description: Strictly nocturnal - you'll never see these flying during daylight hours, they wait until full darkness to become active

idTips.label: Caterpillar Stage
idTips.description: Black woolly bear caterpillar with thick bristles and red or orange bands that become visible when it rolls into a defensive ball - the hairs feel stiff but won't irritate your skin

habitat: Giant Leopard Moths can be found throughout New England in a variety of habitats including gardens, parks, forest edges, and suburban areas. They're often attracted to outdoor lights and may visit gardens where they're drawn to bitter vegetables like unripe tomatoes and broccoli flowers. The caterpillars feed on a wide range of plants, so adults can appear almost anywhere from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring (May), when you might spot them at porch lights or resting on walls during the day after nighttime flights.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for adult moths - they're most active and commonly seen from June through August at lights and occasionally in gardens visiting flowers.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying through September, while woolly bear caterpillars become more visible as they search for overwintering spots.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - caterpillars overwinter and this species takes two full years to complete its life cycle.

funFact: Giant Leopard Moths have marathon mating sessions that last over 24 hours! During this time, the male actually carries the female around like a backpack while she folds up her legs, and they move together to find shade when it's too hot or sun when they're too cold.
confusionNotes: The distinctive leopard-spot pattern makes this moth nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England species. The closest might be some smaller tiger moths, but none have the same crisp white and black leopard pattern combined with the large size.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'leopard' moth, this species is actually in the tiger moth family (Erebidae). The old scientific name Ecpantheria scribonia is sometimes still used, but the current name is Hypercompe scribonia. Like many tiger moths, the adults are nocturnal and the caterpillars are woolly bears.
compareHints: The Giant Leopard Moth is the only species in its genus (Hypercompe) found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other tiger moths in the same family, it's distinguished by its large size, pure white background color, and neat leopard-spot pattern - most other tiger moths have different color schemes like yellow, orange, or cream backgrounds with different marking patterns.
